h1: Hop burn in hazy IPA and the polyphenols behind it
title: Hop Burn in Hazy IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: What causes hop burn in hazy IPA, how polyphenols and hop particles create that harsh throat bite and how to reduce it without losing aroma.
teaser: That scratchy burn at the back of the throat in a fresh hazy IPA is not bitterness. It is hop matter.
standfirst: Hop burn is the harsh, scratchy, peppery sensation in the throat that some heavily dry hopped beers leave behind. It is common in young hazy IPAs. Most of it comes from hop material and polyphenols still floating in the beer, which means it can be managed.
sections:
Hop burn is a physical sensation more than a flavour. Drinkers describe it as a burning, scratchy, prickly or peppery feeling at the back of the throat, sometimes with a drying, chalky astringency on the tongue. It often lingers after swallowing.

It is different from bitterness. Bitterness comes from iso-alpha acids formed in the boil and is tasted on the tongue. A hazy IPA can have modest measured bitterness and still deliver strong hop burn. Our guide to bitterness perception explains how the two get confused.

No single compound has been proven to cause hop burn, but brewers and researchers generally point to a few contributors:

  • Hop particles in suspension. Fine fragments of hop pellet that have not settled out. They carry polyphenols, plant material and oils straight onto the palate.
  • Polyphenols. Hops are rich in polyphenols, which give astringency and harshness. Heavy dry hopping extracts a lot of them, especially with long contact times.
  • Yeast in suspension. Hazy IPAs often hold a lot of yeast, which adds its own bite.
  • High pH. Dry hopping raises beer pH. A higher pH beer can taste harsher and less crisp.
  • Youth. Very fresh beer, packaged within days of dry hopping, has had no time for particles to drop out.

The common thread is suspended material. Beers that have settled well rarely show strong hop burn.

Most hop burn fades as hop material drops out of suspension. Cold conditioning is the main tool. After dry hopping, cool the beer to around 0 to 2 °C and hold it for several days before packaging. The colder and longer, the more settles.

The floor detail that makes cold conditioning work: dump the cone. On a conical fermenter, hop debris and yeast pile up at the bottom. Draw that material off through the bottom valve once or twice during the cold rest, waiting a day between dumps. Leaving it there means it can be stirred back up when you transfer.

Cold conditioning does not mean filtering out the haze. A good hazy IPA keeps its proteins and polyphenol haze, which is fine and stable. The aim is to drop out the coarse hop matter.

• Shorter dry hop contact. Most aroma oil comes out within a day or two. Longer contact extracts more polyphenol and plant material. Remove or drop out the hops once the aroma is there.
  • Lower dry hop rates. Very high rates give diminishing aroma returns and more burn. Better extraction, through rousing and timing, often beats more hops.
  • Hop products with less plant matter. Lupulin concentrated pellets and hop extracts deliver oils with less leaf and stem. They tend to give less burn per unit of aroma.
  • Gentle transfer. Draw beer from above the yeast and hop bed, not from the bottom of the cone.

Our dry hopping guide covers rates and timing in more detail.
Time and freshness in the Indian market

Hop burn usually softens over the first couple of weeks after packaging as particles settle in the can. Hop aroma also fades over the same period, more quickly in warm storage. That puts brewers in a bind. Ship too young and drinkers taste burn. Hold too long and the aroma dulls.

In India, where cold chains are patchy, the answer is to do the settling in the tank, not the can. Cold condition properly, package clear of debris, then get the beer to market cold and fast. Our guide to fresh versus stale IPA covers what happens to hoppy beer in warm storage.

Taste your beer at packaging and again a week later, side by side if you have kept a can cold. Note when the burn fades and how much aroma you lose by then. Compare batches with different contact times or cold conditioning periods. Within a few brews you will know the trade-off on your own system.

Hop burn sits where hop chemistry, yeast behaviour and process timing meet. Understanding the mechanisms, rather than following a rule of thumb, is what lets a brewer get big aroma without the bite.
faqs: A harsh, scratchy or peppery sensation at the back of the throat, common in young, heavily dry hopped beers such as hazy IPA.
Is hop burn the same as bitterness?
No. Bitterness comes from iso-alpha acids formed in the boil. Hop burn comes mainly from suspended hop particles and polyphenols.
How do I reduce hop burn in hazy IPA?
Cold condition at about 0 to 2 °C for several days, dump hop debris from the cone, shorten dry hop contact and avoid very high hop rates.
Does hop burn go away with time?
It usually softens over a week or two as particles settle, but hop aroma fades too, so settling in the tank is the better approach.
